# 10 — Technical Observations: ischedule.MD

**Phase:** 11 — externally observable technical behaviour (frontend stack, routes, API resource patterns, auth/session, real-time, caching/performance), gathered entirely from network and DOM evidence generated by normal, already-verified read-only navigation.

**Purpose boundary:** this report documents only what SchedulePoint may need to support or improve **independently**. It does not reconstruct, copy, or reverse-engineer ischedule.MD's implementation. No source code was accessed; only publicly-served static assets (library names/versions) and the shape of network traffic a normal browser session generates were observed.

**Evidence labels:** **[OBSERVED]** direct browser-visible evidence · **[INFERRED]** reasonable conclusion not directly confirmed · **[UNRESOLVED]** open question.

---

## 1. Executive technical summary

ischedule.MD is a **server-rendered, jQuery/Bootstrap-era multi-page web application** (not a modern SPA framework like React/Angular/Vue) backed by an **ASP.NET-family server** (strong signal: use of Microsoft **SignalR** for real-time features, PascalCase API path segments, `/Content/`, `/Images/`, `/js/` asset conventions with ASP.NET-style bundling cache-busting hashes). The UI is built from **Bootstrap 3.4.1**, **Kendo UI (Telerik) 2014.2.1008**, **jQuery 1.9.1** + **jQuery UI**, **Font Awesome 4.7.0** icon fonts, and a handful of small jQuery plugins (`bootstrap-notify` for toasts, `bootstraptour` for the still-unobserved product tour). Real-time picklist updates are delivered via a **SignalR "picklist" hub**, observed negotiating down to **long-polling** transport rather than WebSockets. A significant, concretely-observed **client-side performance defect** was found: opening a single picklist's detail view fired the **same GET request roughly 25–40 times in immediate succession** — a clear duplicate-request / N+1-style bug, not a security or safety issue, but a real reliability/performance signal SchedulePoint should design against from day one (§10, §13).

## 2. Observation methodology and safety boundary

All evidence in this report was produced by:
- Normal page navigation to screens already established as safe/read-only across Phases 1–10 (My Schedule, Master Schedule, Vacation, Picklist Manager's list and one already-verified-safe detail-row click).
- Passive reading of the browser's own network log (`read_network_requests`) and console log (`read_console_messages`) — no request was constructed, replayed, resent, or modified.
- Passive DOM/JS inspection (`document.cookie` **names only**, `localStorage`/`sessionStorage` **key names only**, script/link tag `src`/`href` values) — no cookie, token, or storage **value** was read or recorded.
- No file was uploaded, downloaded, imported, exported, printed, or opened; the two previously-identified PDFs were not touched.
- No control associated with any of the batch's prohibited action verbs (Add/New/Create/Import/Sync/Upload/Download/Delete/Remove/Save/Submit/Apply/Publish/Approve/Accept/Reject/Withdraw/Transfer/Claim/Assign/Send/Share/Email/SMS/Notify/Start/Stop/Pause/Resume/Complete/Lock/Unlock/Confirm/Update/Edit/Impersonate/Sign in as) was clicked.
- Every identifier below (group, user, picklist, connection token, hashed avatar identifier) is **sanitized** to a placeholder. No live identifier is reproduced where a placeholder would serve equally well for a technical audience.
- **No accidental mutation occurred this phase.**

| Zendesk widget | `assets.zendesk.com/external/zenbox/v2.6/{zenbox.css,zenbox.js}` | **[OBSERVED]** returning **HTTP 503** on every page load tested — the embedded support-chat widget's own assets are currently unavailable from the vendor side (see §12) |

**Rendering approach:** **[OBSERVED]** server-rendered HTML shell per route (`/app`, `/app/schedulenew`, `/vacation/index`, `/admin/picklists` each return a full `200 GET` HTML document, not a single `index.html` shell), with page-specific JS bundles loaded per route (`js/app/home`, `js/app/scheduleNew`, etc.) that then hydrate the page with AJAX-fetched JSON data. This is a **classic server-rendered multi-page application (MPA) with AJAX-enhanced pages**, not a client-side-routed single-page application (SPA).

**Client-side routing:** **[OBSERVED — absent]** every sidebar navigation link triggers a full `GET` to a new server route (confirmed by the network log showing a fresh full-page request, e.g. `GET /vacation/index`, each time the sidebar is used) — there is no client-side router intercepting navigation. **[Consistent with]** the `#groupId=GROUP_ID&...` URL fragment being used for *view state* (date range, selected view mode) layered on top of real server routes, not for SPA routing itself.

**URL state / query parameters:** **[OBSERVED]** the URL hash carries client-only view state (`#groupId=GROUP_ID&weeks=1&view=date&begin=YYYY-MM-DD&batch=off&buildState=all` on Master Schedule) while the path itself (`/app/schedulenew`) is the real server route. This is a hybrid pattern: hash fragment for ephemeral view state, real path for the page itself.

**Form behaviour:** **[UNRESOLVED]** — no form was submitted this phase (per the safety boundary), so actual submission behavior (AJAX vs. full postback) was not directly observed this phase; Phase 4/7's evidence of modals staying open with inline validation-adjacent copy (e.g., the "must be a Monday/Sunday" date constraints on Build Setup) suggests **[INFERRED]** client-side validation exists at least for date-format/business-rule checks, layered in front of whatever server-side validation exists.

**Loading states:** **[OBSERVED, recap from Phase 8]** a "Loading Content" banner and a spinner image (`Images/spinner.gif`) are used during data fetches.

**Error boundaries:** **[UNRESOLVED]** — no client-side error state (e.g., a JS exception surfaced to the user) was encountered in any phase; console logs were clean on every load checked.

**Client-side caching:** **[UNRESOLVED]** — not directly measured this phase (would require comparing response headers across repeated identical requests, which this pass did not capture at the header level); see §10 for the closest available evidence (the duplicate `pickordersadmin` calls, which suggest **no** client-side response caching/deduplication is happening for that endpoint, or it would not have been called dozens of times for identical parameters within one interaction).

**Static assets:** **[OBSERVED]** first-party JS/CSS bundles are served with a `?v=<hash>` cache-busting query string (ASP.NET bundling convention), implying long-lived HTTP caching keyed to content hash — a reasonable, standard pattern.

**CSS/design-system patterns:** **[OBSERVED, recap from Phase 10]** Bootstrap 3 utility classes (`btn btn-default`, `modal`, `dropdown-toggle`) plus Kendo's own theme classes layered on top — a **two-design-system** UI (Bootstrap for layout/buttons, Kendo for data-dense widgets), which explains some of the visual/interaction inconsistency noted in Phase 10 (e.g., some dropdowns are native-feeling Bootstrap, others are clearly Kendo comboboxes with different keyboard/visual behavior).

**Responsive implementation:** **[OBSERVED, recap from Phase 10]** consistent with a Bootstrap-3-era fluid-grid approach (shrink-to-fit calendar, wrapping toolbars) rather than a mobile-first component redesign — matches Bootstrap 3's own responsive philosophy (fluid grid, not distinct mobile components).

**Accessibility-related technical behaviour:** **[OBSERVED, recap from Phase 10]** globally-suppressed focus outlines, missing `aria-label`s on icon-only buttons, absent heading hierarchy — all consistent with an application built primarily against Bootstrap 3 + Kendo 2014-era defaults without a dedicated accessibility remediation pass layered on top.

## 4. Route and navigation patterns

All identifiers sanitized.

| Route family | Pattern | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Personal schedule | `/app` | default landing route |
| Master schedule | `/app/schedulenew` | state in hash: `#groupId=GROUP_ID&weeks=N&view=date\|staff\|shift&begin=YYYY-MM-DD&batch=on\|off&buildState=all` |
| On call | `/app/oncalltoday` | |
| Vacation | `/vacation/index` | note the differing path style (no `/app/` prefix) — a **route-naming inconsistency** worth flagging (§13) |
| Daily assignments | `/app/viewplm` | carries `pickListId` in the URL for a specific date's resolved output |
| Choose list | `/app/picklist` | |
| Contacts | `/app/contacts` | |
| Documents | `/app/documents` | |
| Picklist Manager (admin) | `/admin/picklists` | hash carries `pickListId=PICKLIST_ID` when a row is selected |
| Scheduling admin family | `/admin/groups`, `/admin/builds`, `/admin/staffshiftfte`, `/admin/shiftstatistics`, `/admin/users`, `/admin/staffgroup`, `/admin/shifts`, `/admin/shiftgroup`, `/admin/validgroups`, `/admin/patterns`, `/admin/staffrules` | consistent `/admin/<resource>` family, except two outliers below |
| Build editor | `/admin/schedulebuildsmanagement?buildId=BUILD_ID` | a longer, non-abbreviated route name breaking the short `/admin/<resource>` pattern used elsewhere |
| Pattern/Staff rule editors | `/admin/patternsmanagement`, `/admin/staffRulesmanagement` | same "…management" naming outlier as Build Editor; note **inconsistent casing** — `staffRulesmanagement` (camelCase `R`) vs. `patternsmanagement` (all lowercase) |
| Valid group editor | `/admin/schedulevalidgroupsmanagement?validGroupId=ID` | yet another naming variant (`schedule`-prefixed) for what is otherwise the same "…management" editor pattern |
| Sign-in-as | `/admin/signas` | |
| User self-service | `/users/profile`, `/users/notifications` | a distinct `/users/` family from `/admin/users` (plural resource root reused for both an admin list and a personal-settings namespace — a naming collision worth flagging) |

**Group/tenant context in URLs [OBSERVED]:** every data-bound page carries `groupId=GROUP_ID`, either as a genuine query parameter (API calls) or as a URL hash fragment (page views). **[OBSERVED, §3]** a `SelectedGroupId` cookie also exists, meaning group context is carried **redundantly** in up to three places at once (hash fragment, explicit query param on API calls, and a cookie) for the same page load — **[INFERRED]** the cookie is likely the server-side source of truth (used for the initial server-rendered HTML) while the hash/query param drive subsequent client-side AJAX calls once the page is loaded.

**Date parameters [OBSERVED, concrete inconsistency]:** at least **three different date formats** were observed across sibling API calls in the same session: `YYYY-MM-DD` (ISO, e.g. `workdays`, `VacationYear`), `MM%2FDD%2FYYYY` (URL-encoded `MM/DD/YYYY`, e.g. `works/groupnew`), and `MMM D, YYYY` with a literal comma (e.g. `works/monthly/{userId}?at=Jul 1, 2026`). This is a genuine **API design inconsistency** — three different date serialization conventions for conceptually the same "date" parameter across sibling endpoints, likely reflecting incremental endpoint additions over the product's history rather than a single deliberate API design pass.

**Redirect / deep-link / refresh / direct-navigation behaviour [OBSERVED, recap from Phase 4]:** an authenticated session redirects seamlessly between routes (e.g., clicking "Sign In" from the marketing site while already authenticated lands directly in `/app`); direct navigation to any `/admin/*` or `/app/*` route while authenticated loads that route's content directly (confirmed throughout every phase of this research, since every phase relied on direct URL navigation). **[UNRESOLVED]** unauthenticated deep-link behavior (would require an unauthenticated session, not available — see Phase 4's login-observation limitation).

**Error/unavailable routes [UNRESOLVED]:** no 404 or route-level error page was encountered in any phase (every route navigated to was a real, working route already known from the application map).

**External-link behaviour [OBSERVED, recap]:** Support → `ischedulemd.zendesk.com` (opens the same tab, per Phase 1's observation of the link's plain `<a href>` structure — not `target="_blank"`, based on the link element inspected in earlier phases).

## 6. Sanitized request and response patterns

- **Request shape:** every observed API call this phase was a plain `GET` with parameters in the **query string**, not a JSON request body — consistent with a set of simple, read-oriented REST-ish endpoints layered under `/api/`. **[OBSERVED]** No `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` call was observed (expected, since no mutating action was performed).
- **Response envelope:** **[UNRESOLVED]** — response bodies were not fetched this phase (the browser tool's network-log view did not expose a response-body-fetch path within the safety constraints of this session); response *shape* is therefore inferred only from what the UI subsequently renders, not confirmed at the JSON level. A future authorized pass with header/body inspection tooling could confirm envelope shape (e.g., whether responses are bare arrays, `{data: [...]}`-wrapped, or include pagination metadata).
- **Status codes observed:** `200` (near-universal for first-party API calls), `503` (Zendesk's own third-party assets, twice, consistently — see §12), one request left `pending` at capture-window end (`i0.wp.com` image proxy — see §10).
- **Pagination metadata:** **[INFERRED]** the `pageNumber` parameter on API-12 (VacationYear) is the only direct evidence of a pagination convention; its exact metadata shape (total pages? total items? next/prev links?) is **[UNRESOLVED]** without a response body.
- **Date/time format:** see §4 — **[OBSERVED]** three distinct conventions in use across sibling endpoints (ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`, US `MM/DD/YYYY`, and a human-readable `MMM D, YYYY`). **[UNRESOLVED]** whether responses echo dates back in a fourth, unified format, or mirror the request's own convention.
- **Time zone representation:** **[UNRESOLVED]** — no explicit timezone offset or IANA zone identifier was observed in any request URL; dates appear to be treated as timezone-naive "calendar dates," consistent with a scheduling domain where a shift's "date" matters more than an absolute instant — but this is an inference, not confirmed against a response body.
- **Boolean/status fields:** **[OBSERVED]** query-string booleans use lowercase `true`/`false` literals (e.g., `flag=true&flag2=true`, `allowRequest=true`) — a standard, unremarkable convention.
- **Correlation/request identifiers:** **[OBSERVED]** SignalR long-polling requests carry a `tid` (transport ID) and a cache-busting `_=<timestamp>` parameter, plus a `messageId` on `poll` calls (e.g., `d-A6672EBF-A,12|Ex,0|...`) — this `messageId` is a **SignalR-internal sequencing token**, not a business identifier; its *format* is documented here (dash-and-pipe-delimited) without reproducing a specific live value beyond this one already-sanitized-in-spirit example (the actual captured value contained no personal data, only protocol-internal sequence markers, so its literal form is shown once as a format example; no further live values are reproduced anywhere else in this report).

## 7. Authentication and session behaviour

- **Login redirects [OBSERVED, recap from Phase 4]:** clicking "Sign In" on the marketing homepage while already authenticated redirects straight into `/app` with no credential prompt — session state persists across the marketing/app boundary.
- **Logout behaviour [UNRESOLVED]:** never triggered (Sign Out is in the do-not-click list across every phase, since ending the only available authenticated session would end the research capability with no way back in).
- **Session expiry / idle timeout [UNRESOLVED]:** the session used across all eleven phases of this research (spanning several hours of elapsed wall-clock time within the session) never appeared to expire or prompt re-authentication — **[INFERRED]** either a long session lifetime or a silent token-refresh mechanism, not distinguishable without inspecting cookie *values* (prohibited).
- **Authentication-required redirects [UNRESOLVED]:** never observed, since no unauthenticated request was ever made this session.
- **Group switching [OBSERVED, recap]:** confirmed in Phase 3 to be a client-side context change reflected in the `SelectedGroupId` cookie and the URL hash/query `groupId`, with every subsequent API call re-scoped to the new value — no full re-authentication occurs on group switch.
- **Session refresh behaviour [UNRESOLVED]:** not directly observable without token inspection.
- **Anti-forgery protections [UNRESOLVED]:** no anti-forgery token *name* was observed in any GET request this phase (expected — anti-forgery tokens typically appear on state-changing `POST`/`PUT` requests, none of which were triggered). **[INFERRED]** given the ASP.NET-family backend signal, the framework's standard anti-forgery token mechanism (`__RequestVerificationToken` or ASP.NET Core's equivalent) is a reasonable default assumption for form submissions, but this was not confirmed by observing an actual form POST.
- **Authorization-error presentation [UNRESOLVED]:** never triggered (would require attempting an action outside this account's role, explicitly out of scope — "do not test authorization boundaries").
- **Multiple-tab behaviour [OBSERVED, recap from Phase 4]:** a second tab opened to the marketing site shared the same authenticated session (cookie-based, same browser profile) — confirmed by the "Sign In" click bouncing straight into the app in that second tab without a fresh login.
- **Cookies observed [OBSERVED, names only, no values]:** `remember` and `SelectedGroupId` are both readable via `document.cookie` (i.e., **not** `HttpOnly`). **No session/authentication cookie name was visible to JavaScript** — **[INFERRED]** the actual auth session cookie is `HttpOnly` (a good security practice, hiding it from any client-side script including malicious injected scripts), while `remember` and `SelectedGroupId` are intentionally left script-readable because the app's own client-side code needs to read `SelectedGroupId` for its logic.
- **Local/session storage [OBSERVED]:** both `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` were empty (zero keys) on every screen checked — the app does not use browser storage for client-side state; **all state is server/cookie-driven**. This is a notably conservative, low-attack-surface choice worth deliberately deciding on (not simply copying) for SchedulePoint.

## 8. Real-time and background behaviour

**This is the most significant single finding of this phase**, and it directly closes part of Phase 8's largest evidence gap (picklist real-time behavior) without ever triggering a live picklist.

- **[OBSERVED, high confidence]** Every page load initiates a **SignalR** handshake: `GET /signalr/negotiate?clientProtocol=1.4&connectionData=[{"name":"picklist"}]` → `GET /signalr/connect?transport=longPolling&...` → `GET /signalr/start?transport=longPolling&...` → `POST /signalr/send?transport=longPolling&...` → `GET /signalr/poll?transport=longPolling&messageId=...`. This confirms:
  1. **A dedicated SignalR hub named "picklist" exists** — the real-time mechanism Phase 8 could not directly observe (no active picklist was available across the whole research effort) is confirmed to exist and to be **actively connected on every page load**, not just picklist-specific pages.
  2. **Transport negotiated to long-polling, not WebSockets** — SignalR's own negotiation protocol chose long-polling for this session (**[OBSERVED]** the `transport=longPolling` parameter on every subsequent call). **[UNRESOLVED]** whether this is because WebSockets are unavailable/blocked in this specific browser environment, or whether the server-side SignalR configuration doesn't offer WebSocket transport at all — the negotiation response body itself (which would list available transports) was not inspected.
  3. **A fresh connection (and fresh `connectionToken`) is established on every full page navigation** — not a single persistent connection reused across the whole session. **[OBSERVED]** — this is a reasonable pattern for an MPA (each page load is a fresh document, so a fresh SignalR connection is expected), but means real-time delivery has a gap during page-to-page navigation.
- **Polling frequency:** **[UNRESOLVED]** — the long-polling `poll` request's own response timing (how long the server holds the connection open before responding) was not measured across a sustained period this phase.
- **Background jobs / queued work:** **[OBSERVED, indirect]** the `/api/jobs` and `/api/jobs/JobsForRequest` endpoints (§5, API-03/04) strongly suggest a server-side "jobs" concept distinct from the SignalR push channel — **[INFERRED]** possibly a polling-based fallback or a notification/reminder queue surfaced via regular page-load fetches rather than push.
- **Status polling / long-running report generation / schedule-build status updates:** **[UNRESOLVED]** — the "Create X Report" dialogs (Phase 10) and the Builds pipeline (05-scheduling-engine.md) were never exercised with network capture active, so whether report generation or a schedule Build uses the same SignalR channel, a separate polling mechanism, or a simple synchronous request/response is unknown.
- **Picklist live-update mechanism specifically:** **[INFERRED, moderate-high confidence]** given the hub is literally named "picklist," it is a very reasonable inference that this channel is what pushes live updates (current picker, room selections, completions) to Picklist Manager and the Dashboard monitor during an active draft — but this remains **[UNRESOLVED]** as *confirmed* behavior, since no picklist was ever active to observe an actual message flow through this channel. This is the appropriate, honest boundary given this phase's explicit instruction not to attempt to close that gap.
- **Retry behaviour / idempotency clues / duplicate-request protection:** **[OBSERVED — a negative finding, see §10]** the `pickordersadmin` duplication (called ~25–40 times for one click) shows **no evidence of client-side request deduplication or debouncing** for at least that endpoint. Whether the server has any idempotency handling for repeated identical GETs is moot for a read-only endpoint (repeated identical GETs are safe by HTTP definition) but the sheer volume is a performance concern regardless of safety.

## 9. File, report, calendar, and integration behaviour

- **File-upload architecture [UNRESOLVED]:** the Documents "UpLoad File" and Picklist-related Import controls were never activated (explicitly prohibited); no upload request shape was observed.
- **File-download architecture [UNRESOLVED]:** no file was downloaded (explicitly prohibited); the two "ischedule documents" PDFs remain unopened per instruction.
- **Report-generation behaviour [PARTIALLY OBSERVED via Phase 10's passive discovery]:** the Master Schedule Print menu opens one of five **"Create `<Type>` Report"** dialogs (Schedule, Picklist, Stipend, Requests, and a previously-unknown **DayXShift** type) rather than an instant download — **[OBSERVED]** (via heading-text inspection only, never clicked); the dialogs' own fields, and the network request their eventual submission would generate, remain **[UNRESOLVED]**.
- **Print behaviour [UNRESOLVED]:** no Print control was activated this phase.
- **Calendar-subscription mechanism [OBSERVED, recap from Phase 4]:** a `webcal://` URL containing the user's own email, `groupId`, and an opaque `hash` bearer token — **[OBSERVED]** structure only; the token value was never captured or reproduced, consistent with this phase's rules.
- **Calendar-feed format [INFERRED]:** `webcal://` is the standard scheme for pointing a calendar client at an `.ics` (iCalendar) feed URL — **[INFERRED]** the feed itself very likely serves standard iCalendar-format data, though the feed's actual response was never fetched (would require following the link, not done).
- **Export mechanisms [OBSERVED, recap from Phase 9]:** Contacts' "Export" button and the various Print-menu items are the only export-shaped controls found; none activated, none inspected at the network level.
- **Import mechanisms [OBSERVED, recap from Phase 8]:** Picklist Manager's "Import" buttons are confirmed **not** file-uploads — they trigger a confirm-dialog-gated **re-sync from an internal source**, not a client-to-server file transfer. No corresponding network request was captured this phase (the confirm dialog was not accepted, consistent with "do not activate Import").
- **External integration patterns [OBSERVED, recap + new]:** Zendesk (support widget, currently `503`-erroring — see §12), Gravatar (avatar images, hashed identifier sent to a third party — see §14), Google Fonts, Bootstrap CDN, Cloudflare cdnjs, a Cloudfront-hosted Kendo UI asset bucket, and WordPress.com's Jetpack/Photon image proxy (`i0.wp.com`) for at least one avatar-image request. **No SSO, EHR, or paging-system integration** was observed anywhere in the network traffic across any phase of this research — consistent with Phase 9's finding that no such integration exists in the UI either.

## 10. Caching and performance observations

- **[OBSERVED, significant] Duplicate-request defect:** selecting a single picklist row in Picklist Manager triggered **~25–40 identical `GET /api/pickordersadmin?pickListId=PICKLIST_ID` requests** in immediate succession, confirmed stable (not still growing) after an additional 3-second wait with no further user action. **[INFERRED]** the most likely cause, given the count is in the same rough range as the picklist's own staff-row count (~18 in the observed instance, though the request count exceeded that), is a client-side rendering bug where each row (or some per-row/per-cell component) independently re-fetches the same list resource instead of reading from a single shared fetch — a classic N+1 pattern at the AJAX layer rather than the database layer, but with the same class of impact (wasted server load, wasted client bandwidth, slower perceived responsiveness). One request in the burst used a differently-named parameter (`Id=` instead of `pickListId=`), suggesting at least two different code paths independently trigger calls to the same endpoint.
- **[OBSERVED]** A third-party avatar-image request (`i0.wp.com`) remained in a `pending` state through the end of a normal page-load capture window — a mild but real reliability signal for a dependency that isn't even first-party.
- **[OBSERVED]** Zendesk's own CSS/JS assets consistently return `503` — an always-broken third-party embed on every single page load, silently failing (no visible error surfaced to the user in any screenshot across ten prior phases) — see §12.
- **Repeated requests across navigations [OBSERVED]:** the same core data fetches (`users`, `jobs`, `works`, `workdays`) were re-issued on every single page navigation observed, even when navigating between pages that plausibly need overlapping data (e.g., Master Schedule → Vacation both need the user roster) — **[INFERRED]** no cross-page client-side cache is being reused for these; each page independently re-fetches its own roster/schedule data. This is consistent with §7's MPA architecture (each navigation is a fresh document load, so a fresh JS execution context with no in-memory cache is expected) but means **every single navigation pays the full data-fetch cost again** — a real, structural performance consideration.
- **Large responses / slow page loads / N+1 patterns beyond pickordersadmin:** **[UNRESOLVED]** — no response size or load-time measurement was taken this phase (would require Performance/Timing API inspection, not attempted).
- **Lazy loading / prefetching:** **[UNRESOLVED]** — not directly tested.
- **Polling frequency:** see §8 — **[UNRESOLVED]**.

## 12. Observable errors and broken endpoints

- **[OBSERVED, concrete]** `assets.zendesk.com/external/zenbox/v2.6/zenbox.css` and `.../zenbox.js` both return **HTTP 503** on every page load tested across this phase (and, retrospectively, this pattern was present but not flagged as an error in prior phases' screenshots — the support widget simply never rendered, and no user-visible error was shown for it). This is a **live, currently-broken third-party integration** — the in-app support/chat widget has been silently non-functional for at least the duration of this research.
- **[OBSERVED]** one third-party image request (`i0.wp.com`) left pending/unresolved within a normal page-load window.

## 13. SchedulePoint implications

| # | Observation | SchedulePoint must support | SchedulePoint should improve | Security | Privacy | Reliability | Performance | Accessibility | Architectural requirement | Suggested test |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T-01 | Duplicate `pickordersadmin`-style request burst (§10) | Fetching list data needed by multiple UI rows | **Do not** re-fetch the same resource per-row; fetch once, share via a single client-side store/cache | — | — | Wasted server capacity under load | Real, measurable — up to ~40x the necessary request volume for one interaction | — | Every data-fetching component must read from a shared request cache/de-duper, never issue its own independent identical fetch | Automated: assert exactly one network call per unique (endpoint, params) tuple per user interaction, in an integration/E2E test harness |
| T-02 | Inconsistent date formats across sibling endpoints (§4, §6) | Accepting/returning dates in at least the formats a scheduling domain needs (calendar dates, not instants, per §6) | Standardize on **one** date serialization format (ISO 8601 `YYYY-MM-DD`) across every endpoint from day one | — | — | — | — | — | API contract: all date parameters and fields use ISO 8601 exclusively | Automated: schema/contract test rejecting any non-ISO date field |
| T-03 | Inconsistent parameter naming (`pickListId` vs `Id`, boolean `flag`/`flag2`) (§5, §10) | — | Use descriptive, consistent parameter names across all endpoints for the same underlying value | — | — | — | — | — | API design review gate: no endpoint may introduce an undocumented/ambiguous parameter name | Manual: API contract review checklist item |
| T-04 | Route-naming inconsistency (`/vacation/index` vs. `/app/*`; `...management` suffix inconsistently applied/cased) (§4) | — | Adopt one consistent route-naming scheme (e.g., always `/app/<feature>` or a fully resource-based REST path) from the start | — | — | — | — | — | Route-naming convention documented and enforced via lint/review | Automated: route-naming lint rule |
| T-05 | Third-party Gravatar dependency sends a hashed user identifier off-platform for every avatar render (§3, §14) | Displaying user avatars | Do not call an external avatar service with any user-derived identifier (hashed or not) unless explicitly disclosed and consented to; prefer self-hosted or opt-in avatars | **Medium** — a hashed email is a known-reversible identifier via rainbow-table lookup against Gravatar's own service | **Medium-High** — silently sends user PII (in hashed form) to a third party on every page load, for every user, with no apparent opt-out observed | — | — | — | Privacy-by-design requirement: no third-party network call may carry user-derived data without an explicit, documented consent/disclosure mechanism | Manual: privacy review of every third-party network call at launch; automated: CI check flagging any new third-party domain in network calls |
| T-06 | Auth session cookie not readable via `document.cookie`; `remember`/`SelectedGroupId` are | Session persistence, "remember me," and group-context persistence | **Preserve** the `HttpOnly` pattern for the real session/auth cookie — this is good practice, worth carrying forward deliberately, not by accident | **Low priority, but preserve** — this is already a strength to maintain | — | — | — | — | Auth cookies must be `HttpOnly` and `Secure`; only non-sensitive UI-state cookies may be script-readable | Automated: cookie-attribute test (HttpOnly/Secure flags) in CI |
| T-07 | Zero localStorage/sessionStorage usage (§7) | State persistence for UX conveniences (draft form data, view preferences) | This is a reasonable, low-attack-surface starting point; if SchedulePoint *does* use client storage, ensure no session/auth data or PII is ever placed there | **Preserve the constraint if adopted; if abandoned, do so deliberately** | Client storage is JS-readable by any script on the page (including XSS payloads) — a smaller attack surface than ischedule.md's own choice, worth keeping | — | — | — | Any future client-storage usage requires an explicit security review before merging | Automated: CI check scanning for `localStorage`/`sessionStorage` writes of anything resembling a token/PII field name |
| T-08 | Zendesk widget silently broken (503) with no user-visible fallback (§12) | Third-party integration failures | Any embedded third-party widget must fail gracefully with a visible, user-understandable fallback (e.g., "Support chat unavailable — email us instead"), never fail silently | — | — | **Medium** — a support channel has been invisibly unavailable, which the product owner may not even know about without traffic inspection like this | — | — | Third-party widget loading must be wrapped in error/timeout handling with a visible fallback UI state | Automated: synthetic monitoring alert on third-party asset failures; manual: periodic support-widget health check |
| T-09 | No client-side router; every navigation is a full page reload (§3) | Full navigability without JS (progressive enhancement floor) | Consider whether a client-side-routed SPA/hybrid (with proper loading states and back/forward support) better serves SchedulePoint's UX goals, or whether an MPA is a deliberate, acceptable choice — **do not default to either without a decision** | — | — | An MPA has a natural resilience advantage (no client-side router state to get stuck) | Full-page reloads re-fetch everything every time (§10) — a real cost at MPA-scale that a well-cached SPA could avoid | Full page reloads reset focus/scroll position every time, a Phase-10-relevant accessibility/UX cost | Explicit architectural decision required, documented with rationale, not inherited by default | Manual: architecture decision record (ADR) for MPA vs. SPA choice |
| T-10 | SignalR "picklist" hub connects on every page load, even non-picklist pages (§8) | Real-time updates scoped to where they're actually needed | Only open a real-time connection on pages that need it, to reduce unnecessary always-on connections | — | — | Fewer always-on connections = fewer things that can silently fail | Reduces idle connection/server overhead at scale | — | Real-time connections must be page/feature-scoped, not global | Automated: assert no real-time connection is opened on pages without a live-updating feature |

## 14. Security and privacy observations

- **[OBSERVED]** the auth/session cookie is not exposed to `document.cookie` (likely `HttpOnly`) — a genuine positive security practice, explicitly not undermined by this research (its value was never inspected, consistent with the rules).
- **[OBSERVED]** a hashed user identifier is sent to Gravatar (a third party) on every avatar render, with a same-origin fallback image URL also passed as a parameter to that same third-party request — meaning even the fallback path leaks the request to Gravatar's servers first. **[INFERRED]** this hash is very likely an MD5 of the user's email (Gravatar's standard, documented convention), which is a **reversible/correlatable identifier** via any of the many public "reverse Gravatar hash" lookup services — a real, if low-severity, privacy leak of "this email address is associated with this healthcare-scheduling product" to a third party, on every page load, for every user, with no apparent consent mechanism observed anywhere in this research.
- **[OBSERVED]** no anti-forgery token name was visible on any GET request (expected — see §7); **[UNRESOLVED]** whether POST/PUT/DELETE requests carry one, since none was triggered.
- **[OBSERVED]** localStorage/sessionStorage are unused — a smaller client-side attack surface than many modern SPAs.
- **[OBSERVED, recap from Phases 1–8]** the product's own UI already surfaces the deepest security-relevant findings of this whole eleven-phase research effort — the "Sign In As" impersonation feature, the vendor-domain "Super"-named account, and the type-to-confirm irreversible Vacation-transfer action — all of which are UI-level, not network-level, findings and are not repeated in full here; see 02-role-permission-matrix.md and 06-requests-vacation-opportunities.md for the complete record.
- **No credential, token value, cookie value, session/local/storage value, or patient/personal data value was captured, recorded, or reproduced anywhere in this report.**
